question: Does oadec's model of the decoder buffer give the figures Dolby's own TrueHD encoder reports for the streams it writes?
method: Dolby Media Encoder 5.7.2's TrueHD encoder (dee_dthd_encoder) on synthetic programmes -- pink noise gated on and off against a tone, so the buffer fills ahead of the loud stretches -- and on an object scene written by oadec atmos-author, each encode with --extras log_format=txt, which keeps the encoder's verification report. tools/fifo_oracle.py reads the report and compares it with oadec verify --json. The encoder refuses 44.1 and 192 kHz input ('Unsupported sample-rate'), so those rates are not in the sample. The logs are not committed; the figures below are the only part of them recorded.

model.arrival: an access unit enters whole at its input_timing (Dolby 2.7), the 16-bit field unwrapped
model.output: the output_timing of the restart headers at a major sync, one frame later for every unit after it (Dolby 2.7)
model.removal: one frame after the output time: removal at the output time misses every reported depth
model.substream_depth: the bytes of the substream's segments, without its directory entry
model.decoder_depth: the segments and the directory entries of the substreams the decoder reads, and the header, major sync and extra data of every unit
model.allowed_substream_depth: 15 000 bytes per channel the restart header spans, as every report states it
model.data_rate: a unit's bits over the input interval to the next unit (Dolby 2.7), rounded to the bit per second like the report; the maximum is the first unit that reaches it

encodes.encode: objects from oadec atmos-author, 48 kHz, 2 s

result.calibration: removal at the output time, and the directory entry counted in a substream's own depth, were the readings the first encode refuted; every other figure fixed the reading above

corpus.where: Coco (2017) and The Incredibles (2004), whose real damage sits at their branch points: all 340 delay and 25 rate findings of Coco lie in its damage regions; none on the 55 streams without damage, the 18 branches of Up (2009) and six encoder-written deliveries included

reading: The model is Dolby's: on five encodes -- two rates, two to four substreams, objects, a rate-optimised encode -- every figure the encoder's verifier prints comes out the same, 35 comparisons, down to the unit a peak is first reached at. The allowance of 15 000 bytes a channel is the encoder's own, stated in each report. Its rules warn: they describe the stream's delivery rather than its content, and on real material they fire only where the stream is already damaged.
